title: App Promo Videos: 10 Concepts for Launches and Ads
summary: Plan app promo video ads for Meta around one complete in-app task, readable screens, 9:16 and 4:5 cuts, and the install or reopen action the campaign is buying.
body_markdown:
An app promo video ad on Facebook and Instagram has to show three things quickly: who the app is for, what changes for them, and enough of the real interface to make that believable. Everything else, from the hook to the cut length, follows from the campaign the ad is made for. A video that persuades a stranger to install is a different piece of work from one that brings back someone who already has the app.


An app ad is not a screen recording with music. It is an argument, and the interface is the evidence. If you want app ads made for you, Knowlify is the done-for-you option we recommend: our team scripts, produces and edits[video ads](https://knowlify.com/video-ad-production) for Facebook and Instagram, and a person checks every ad before delivery.


## Which Meta campaign is the video for?


Decide the campaign before writing the script, because each one asks the video for a different kind of proof.


Campaign goal Meta setup What the video must show


New installs App promotion campaign, including Advantage+ app campaigns The problem and the first useful task in the app


Bring existing users back App engagement campaign A feature, update or reason worth reopening for


An in-app action, such as a subscription App promotion optimized for an in-app event The action, its result and any real offer


Optimizing for an in-app event needs that event measured, through Meta's SDK or a mobile measurement partner. Confirm the measurement before production so the ads are judged on the action they were made to drive.


[Meta's guide to Advantage+ app campaigns](https://www.facebook.com/business/help/2755245231412782) explains that targeting in those campaigns is limited to operating system, country and language, and placements are not chosen by hand. The creative set therefore does more of the work of reaching the right people. Supply concepts that speak to different users and situations, in every aspect ratio, rather than several near-identical edits of one idea. For people who already have the app, Meta's[app engagement campaign](https://www.facebook.com/business/help/466848530089944) guide covers the setup.


## Ten app ad concepts for Meta


1. Old workflow versus the app's workflow
2. One-feature proof
3. A role-specific use case
4. An integration trigger and its automated result
5. A new-feature launch for existing users
6. A template or use-case gallery
7. A product update recap
8. An authorized customer result
9. A common objection, answered on screen
10. A reminder for people who visited but did not install


Each concept answers a different question a viewer might have. Choose a few with distinct jobs before producing variations of any one of them.


## What should the first seconds show?


Show the person, the situation and the app working. Start with a recognizable problem, a desired result or the product doing something useful, not a slow logo animation. Plan for viewers who watch without sound: put the key line on screen as well as in the voiceover, and make sure the interface itself tells the story when muted.


Write the hook after choosing the concept. An opening that grabs attention but has nothing to do with the task wastes the seconds the product needs. Our[video ad hooks framework](https://knowlify.com/articles/video-ad-hooks) organizes openings by the viewer's intent.


## Build one ad around a complete app task


Consider a fictional reading-list app with a confirmed ability to save a link into a named collection. The useful task is not "be more organized"; it is "save this article where I can find it for the project." That task gives the opening, the demonstration and the call to action a shared purpose.


An illustrative opening could show someone hunting for a link among unrelated messages, with the line, "Where did you save the article for this project?" The product section then shows the real save action, the collection name and the saved item in its destination. The ending invites the viewer to install and try collections, an action that actually exists.


Do not imply that the app reads, summarizes or tags the article unless those features are confirmed. A generated transition that appears to extract information from the page can create that impression without a word being said. Review both the narration and the visuals against the approved feature list.


Show the final state. A capture that ends as the user taps "Save" leaves the result ambiguous. Hold on the collection long enough to show where the item went, then stop.


## Capture readable app footage


Prepare a sample account for the recording, with invented but realistic names and content. Make the demonstrated state reproducible, so a correction does not mean rebuilding the account, and note which app version the footage shows. Remove personal information, staging artifacts, notifications, loading delays and irrelevant navigation.


Write a capture plan listing the starting screen, the action and the ending screen for each beat. Capture with the final framing in mind. A phone frame can give context, but it should not shrink the important control into decoration. For a small control, use a clear crop or callout while keeping enough of the surrounding interface to orient the viewer. Never swap real labels for invented ones because they fit the design better.


Capture item Detail to record Approval question


Starting state Which account and collection are visible Can this state be reproduced?


User action The exact control being used Is the action supported in this version?


Result Saved item and destination Does the ending prove the stated task?


Conditions Required setup or plan Does the edit keep the relevant context?
